title: Strength Gain
subtitle: 35 g+ protein, 30%+ of calories from protein
summary: Protein-dense blends to help you build and keep muscle. Most include creatine or leucine-rich whey.
guidance: Aim for roughly 0.7–1 g of protein per pound of body weight a day, spread over 3–5 meals. A smoothie with 35–45 g covers one of those meals. Creatine monohydrate at 3–5 g a day is the most studied supplement for strength; timing matters less than taking it daily.

title: Weight Gain
subtitle: 550 kcal+ with 30 g+ protein
summary: Calorie-dense but whole-food based: oats, nut butters, fruit and dairy rather than sugar.
guidance: A surplus of about 250–500 kcal a day supports lean weight gain. Drinking one of these between meals adds calories without making you too full for your next meal.

title: Fat Loss
subtitle: 350 kcal or less, 25 g+ protein, 5 g+ fiber
summary: High protein and fiber keep you full on fewer calories. Vegetables add volume you won't taste.
guidance: Protein and fiber are the two most filling nutrients. Frozen cauliflower, zucchini and spinach thicken a smoothie for almost no calories. Use these as a meal replacement, not on top of meals.

title: Low Calorie
subtitle: 250 kcal or less, still 15 g+ protein
summary: Light snacks that still deliver protein, so they hold you over.
guidance: Good as a snack or alongside a small meal. Ice and frozen fruit give a thick texture without adding calories.

title: High Calorie
subtitle: 650 kcal+ with 30 g+ protein
summary: Full meals in a glass for hard training days, hard gainers and endurance athletes.
guidance: These are meal-sized. If one feels like too much, split it into two servings across the day.

title: Increased Energy
subtitle: 30 g+ carbs plus natural caffeine or nitrates
summary: Steady carbs paired with coffee, matcha, green tea or beets for a lift without a crash.
guidance: Most healthy adults can have up to 400 mg of caffeine a day. A cup of cold brew has roughly 100–200 mg and a teaspoon of matcha about 70 mg. Skip caffeine within 8 hours of bedtime, and avoid it if you are pregnant or have been told to limit it.

title: Low Carb
subtitle: 15 g or less net carbs, 20 g+ protein
summary: Berries, avocado, greens and protein. Net carbs are total carbs minus fiber.
guidance: If you follow a strict ketogenic diet, check the net carbs against your own daily limit. Avocado and nut butters make these creamy without fruit sugar.

title: High Carb
subtitle: 65 g+ carbs, 15 g or less fat
summary: For carb-loading, endurance days and refilling glycogen, from fruit, oats and dates.
guidance: Endurance athletes often need 5–10 g of carbs per kg of body weight a day on heavy training days. Lower fat keeps these quick to digest.

title: Pre-Workout
subtitle: 30 g+ carbs, light on fat and fiber
summary: Easy-to-digest fuel to drink 30–90 minutes before training.
guidance: Fat and fiber slow digestion, so these keep both low to avoid a heavy stomach. Drink 30–90 minutes before you train. Beets and spinach supply nitrates, which may help endurance.

title: Post-Workout
subtitle: 30 g+ protein and 35 g+ carbs
summary: Protein to repair muscle and carbs to refill energy stores.
guidance: Within about two hours after training, 25–40 g of protein with some carbs supports recovery. Tart cherries have been studied for reducing muscle soreness.

title: Intra-Workout
subtitle: Light, hydrating carbs with electrolytes
summary: Thin, sippable blends for sessions longer than about an hour.
guidance: For sessions over 60–75 minutes, 30–60 g of carbs an hour plus sodium helps keep energy up. Blend with extra water or ice so they're easy to sip from a bottle. Shorter sessions only need water.
